title: Lifetimes
summary: How the compiler makes sure references never outlive their data - what a lifetime is, lifetime annotations on functions like longest, the elision rules that let you leave most of them out, structs that hold references, lifetimes in impl blocks and methods, 'static, and practical ways out such as returning owned data.

cards.q: What does `fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` promise?
cards.a:
The result is valid while both inputs are, so it may borrow from either

One lifetime for all three means the result can only be used while both inputs are still alive: the shorter of the two lifetimes.

cards.q: Why does `fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` need no lifetime annotation?
cards.a:
With one input reference, elision gives the output that same lifetime

The elision rules fill in `fn first_word<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &'a str`. With two input references, like `longest`, you must write them.

cards.q: What is the type of the literal `"hello"`?
cards.a:
&'static str

Literals are stored in the program binary and live for the whole run.
